content:
"Instead of tossing pruned branches from your winter tidy-up onto the bonfire or through a shredder, give them a second life by building a dead hedge. This simple structure makes an excellent windbreak, offers fantastic shelter for birds and insects, and creates a natural boundary within your garden. Drive in sturdy stakes or reclaimed fence posts in two parallel lines about 50cm apart, then stack your cuttings between them, starting with the thickest pieces at the bottom for stability. Keep adding material as it becomes available; the pile will compress gradually over time.

If the holidays left you empty-handed, consider treating yourself by pre-ordering The Book of Seeds (Ivy Press, £30) by Paul Smith, the former head of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank. Due out in February, this lavish volume showcases 600 remarkable seeds from around the globe—ranging from a glossy black specimen with a shock of hair reminiscent of a certain famous coiffure to orchid seeds so tiny they’re no bigger than a pinhead.

For winter color, few climbers rival clematis that bloom in the cold months. In a warm, protected, sunny spot, Clematis cirrhosa varieties can flower from December through February. Try C. cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ (3m x 1.5m) or C. cirrhosa var. balearica (2.5m x 1.5m) for cream, scented bells flecked with maroon, or opt for C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’ for pure white blooms, reaching around 5m x 2m. Is there anything else I can help with?"
